I'm in general agreement. This same kind of experiment has been done repeatedly for decades--in addition to over a century of arctic and antarctic expeditions and continuous stations, any number of military isolation experiments, underwater habitats, sub duty, and so on. I really don't grasp what new insights are expected. If the point is ultimately just catalyzing public interest, then do something the public can participate in.

One of the interesting things about likely space architecture is that large, truly permanent habitats are actually most-likely to be based on very simple, mostly windowless, structures; big excavated spaces, built-up domes of concrete-like material covered in regolith. And these are spaces people will be spending virtually all their time in, relying predominantly on telerobots to do things outside out of both safety and simple convenience. So that means two things; first, the chief design problem for living well in space is figuring out how to live comfortably when you're indoors 99.99% of the time--with one of the obvious solutions the creation of an 'interior outdoors' through horticulture. Second, these spaces will be outfit for habitation by retrofit because they can't be easily modified and so have to be as adaptive as possible. Functionally generic architecture. And whatever you can't make locally, you have to bring in small packages that can fit through an airlock. For the most part, you can't precision-fabricate anything in space that you can't fit through an airlock. Now, this is a very interesting point because it means that the design of a space settlement is mostly interior design using stuff at a human scale that is largely independent of the primary structures providing shelter. Consequently, any simple large-span spaces you might have available here on Earth; prefab domes, mining complexes, airliner or airship hangars, you name, are perfectly suitable analogs for these eventual habitat environments. You don't need million dollar engineering facilities to work on these interior designs. All you need is a model of the logistical situation and some idea of the likely mix of materials that would be available produced by in-situ resource utilization--which, interestingly, are rather similar to those common to traditional pre-industrial Japanese culture.

So, for some time, I've proposed this idea for a kind of home and garden show of space called Space@Home. The idea is to borrow a space like the Kansas City Subtropolis and invite pro, student, and amateur designers and makers to come in and craft their own visions for what living in space would be like. That's something many people could participate in, would stimulate a lot of creativity and public thought about space settlement, and which the general public could readily visit and explore. This would be a very fun, easy, and practical project to do, but it's never occurred to NASA or any existing space advocacy group because, truth be told, they don't really want the public to participate in any significant way. They just want a fan club waving pennants outside the space center fences.
